scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated as the 'Mule Walk' in the 1910s, inspired by James P. Johnson's stride piano music.
Johnson based the composition on country and square dances he witnessed at The Jungles Casino around 1913.
In 1965, Killer Joe Piro was hired by Smirnoff Vodka to modernize the dance to promote a new drink.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a social expression of the stride music scene in Harlem, it became a commercial fad in the 1960s.
The movements 'lamely portray a mule walking,' serving as a playful, mimetic interpretation of the animal's gait.
Today it is a historical tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers start facing their partner with feet apart.
The right hand is lifted high with a bent elbow, then brought down vigorously as the right knee is lifted to hip height, leaning the chest forward.
This is repeated on the left side.
Watch for The Mule Walk, Mule Flap.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (X5TEsdb918c)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Partners facing each other; involves turning in place.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary musical style is stride piano, a derivative of ragtime featuring a strong, syncopated beat.
Key recordings include James P. Johnson's 'Mule Walk' and Skitch Henderson's 1965 album 'Skitch Plays The Mule,' which features orchestral arrangements and vocal instructions for mixing drinks.
Listen for the Piano, Orchestra.
The pulse is 2/4 or 4/4.

A driving stride piano sound characterized by a steady bass rhythm and highly syncopated melodies. The 1960s version includes orchestral elements and vocalists who describe making a vodka drink over the music.

Listen later: Mule Walk — James P. Johnson; Skitch Plays The Mule — Skitch Henderson

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: In its 1910s form, it was a social dance performed in casinos and dance halls.
By 1965, it was marketed as a club and party dance, often associated with the 'mod' aesthetic of the era as seen in Smirnoff advertisements featuring Killer Joe Piro.

scenes.title: The people
narration: James P. Johnson is the composer of the original music.
Killer Joe Piro, a famous 1960s dance instructor, created the 1965 version.
The dance transitioned from the urban 'Jungles Casino' environment of New York in the 1910s to a national American fad in the 1960s through mass media and advertising.
The Mule is a subclass of social dance, descending from early 20th-century square dances and country steps, evolving through the stride piano era into a 1960s novelty fad.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Stand straight with feet a few inches apart facing a partner.
Step 2: Lift right hand overhead with elbow bent and palms forward.
Footwork from the sources: Alternating knee lifts to hip height with feet coming down to a neutral stance; later includes kicks.
Drill: March in place to a 2/4 stride beat.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Lift right knee to hip height while bringing the right arm down and chest forward.
Step 4: Straighten body and bring foot down while raising the left hand overhead.
Drill: Lift knee to hip height on the accented 2nd count.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
